data.title: Valley Community Healthcare to Host Two Voter Events in October
data.description:
Valley Community Healthcare to Host Two Voter Events in October

Valley Community Healthcare to Host Two Voter Events in October

PR Newswire

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 17, 2026

Free, public gatherings in North Hills and North Hollywood will offer voting services, music, refreshments, fresh produce distribution while supplies last, and seasonal Halloween crafts for all ages.

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Valley Community Healthcare (VCH) will host two Voter events this October in partnership with the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk's Mobile Voting Program. These free, public events will bring convenient voting services directly to the community in a welcoming, family-friendly atmosphere, with music, refreshments, fresh produce distribution while supplies last, and seasonal Halloween crafts for all ages. 

Open to everyone, Valley Voter Fests welcome both current Valley Community Healthcare patients and members of the broader community. Attendees can vote in person, submit a conditional voter registration, drop off their ballots, use an accessible voting device, and access voting assistance and materials in multiple languages.

The first Valley Voter Fest will take place Saturday, October 24, at VCH's North Hills location, followed by a second event Friday, October 30, at its North Hollywood clinic. Free produce and refreshments will be available while supplies last.  Location information below.

Valley Voter Fest Details

North Hills

Saturday, October 24, 2026
9 a.m. to 3 p.m.

Valley Community Healthcare
9119 Haskell Avenue
North Hills, CA 91343

North Hollywood

Friday, October 30, 2026
11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Valley Community Healthcare
6801 Coldwater Canyon Avenue
North Hollywood, CA 91605

For additional voting information, visit LAVOTE.GOV.

To learn more about Valley Community Healthcare and its services, visit vchcare.org. Community members interested in becoming VCH patients can call (818) 763-8836 to speak with an enrollment specialist.

About Valley Community Healthcare

Valley Community Healthcare (VCH) is a nonprofit, Federally Qualified Health Center (FQHC) committed to improving the health and well-being of its community by providing high-quality, comprehensive healthcare services, regardless of ability to pay. With clinics in North Hollywood and North Hills, VCH serves individuals and families throughout the San Fernando Valley and surrounding communities.

data.title: State Licensed Marijuana Operators Will Face Long Delays for DEA Federal Registrations
data.description:
WASHINGTON, D.C. / ACCESS Newswire / October 17, 2026 / MMJ International Holdings, a pharmaceutical development company pursuing FDA regulated cannabinoid medicines for Huntington's disease and multiple sclerosis, today explained why it is challenging the federal government's April 2026 marijuana rescheduling order in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.

The explanation follows public remarks by former Drug Enforcement Administration official Matthew Strait, who said during a recent regulatory webinar that DEA should not be issuing registrations to state licensed marijuana businesses while legal challenges to the new framework remain unresolved.

"My opinion is there should be a healthy dose of expectation management here, because I don't think it would be wise for DEA to issue any registrations," Strait said. He also said DEA had issued "zero" registrations under the new framework at the time of the discussion. The webinar was hosted by attorney Jason Adelstone of Harris Sliwoski and included Gillian Schauer, executive director of the Cannabis Regulators Association (CANNRA). Strait's remarks reflect his personal views, not an official agency position.

MMJ Is Not Challenging Whether Marijuana Can Be Medicine. It Is Challenging How the Government Got Here.

MMJ's challenge does not ask the court to decide whether cannabinoids have medical value. MMJ has spent years and more than $10 million pursuing that question through the only process federal law recognizes: FDA clinical development under DEA oversight.

MMJ's challenge rests on four points:

  1. The order bypassed the process Congress required. Under the Controlled Substances Act, rescheduling a drug requires a scientific and medical evaluation and formal rulemaking on the record. DEA's own formal hearing on marijuana rescheduling ran from June 29 to July 15, 2026. It has not produced even a recommended decision, and the proceeding is currently stayed. Yet the April order had already moved state-licensed medical marijuana into Schedule III.
  2. The order lets a state license substitute for federal standards. Pharmaceutical developers must prove product consistency, stability, manufacturing controls and clinical evidence before their medicines reach patients. The April order gives Schedule III treatment to products distributed through state medical programs that were never required to meet those standards.
  3. The government's own evidence undercuts the order. At the DEA hearing, Dr. Dominic Chiapperino, an FDA official called by the government, agreed on cross-examination that marijuana is "not a single chemical with a consistent and reproducible chemical profile or predictable and consistent clinical effects." A DEA pharmacologist, testifying under restrictions DEA imposed to limit her cross-examination, stated that marijuana is a complex substance that needed a five part evaluation.
  4. Treaty obligations still apply. The United States is bound by the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, which imposes specific controls on cannabis cultivation, manufacture and distribution. MMJ's position is that a framework built around existing state markets does not satisfy those obligations.

Why Registrations Should Wait

Strait's warning reflects a practical reality. Several factors weigh against DEA issuing registrations under the new framework before the courts rule:

  • The framework's legality is unresolved. Petitioners in the D.C. Circuit challenge whether the rescheduling order complies with the Controlled Substances Act, meaning registrations issued under a disputed framework would rest on precarious ground.
  • Undoing registrations would be slow, burdensome and expensive. Revoking a DEA registration generally requires an order to show cause and an opportunity for a hearing; if the court vacates the order later, DEA would face cumbersome, case-by-case revocation proceedings across numerous state operators.
  • Businesses and regulators need certainty, not reversals. Operators who build compliance programs, supply chains, and financing around a federal registration that may later be withdrawn face severe disruption, as do the state regulators overseeing them.
  • The litigation will take time. With briefing schedules underway, a ruling on the merits is months away, leaving any registration issued in the interim legally exposed.

Pending litigation does not automatically bar DEA from acting. But issuing consequential registrations before the courts decide whether the framework is lawful invites exactly the disruption the government says it wants to avoid.

What MMJ Has Built

MMJ's drug product is a finished medicine: a standardized THC/CBD soft-gelatin capsule in final dosage form, reproducible and stable, manufactured for eventual use in clinical trials through a pharmaceutical manufacturing partner. The company holds FDA Investigational New Drug applications for its Huntington's disease and multiple sclerosis programs and an FDA Orphan Drug Designation for its Huntington's disease program. Through the IND process, MMJ is seeking to demonstrate the safety and efficacy of its investigational medicines.

Statement from Duane Boise, President and CEO

"We are not anti-marijuana. We are anti-bad science and anti-fake process."

"MMJ has spent years doing what federal law requires: building a standardized medicine, documenting its manufacture, and submitting it to FDA review. We did that because patients with Huntington's disease and multiple sclerosis deserve medicines backed by evidence, not marketing."

"The April order treats a state license as a substitute for that work. A company that never ran a clinical trial, never validated its manufacturing and never proved its product is consistent from batch to batch now receives federal treatment that the law reserves for drugs with accepted medical use. That is not reform. It is a shortcut, and it devalues the pathway every legitimate drug developer has to follow."

"Matthew Strait is right that expectations need to be managed. If DEA issues registrations and the court then vacates this framework, the agency will have to unwind them one proceeding at a time. Waiting for the court to rule is not obstruction. It is common sense."

"The Controlled Substances Act is not optional. We are asking the court to require the government to follow it."

About the Litigation

MMJ International Holdings is among the petitioners in consolidated proceedings in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit challenging the federal marijuana rescheduling order published at 91 Fed. Reg. 22,714. The challenges remain pending, and the validity of the framework is a matter for the court to decide.

About MMJ International Holdings

MMJ International Holdings is a pharmaceutical development company focused on investigational cannabinoid medicines for serious neurological disorders, including Huntington's disease and multiple sclerosis. The company pursues FDA-regulated clinical development and federal controlled-substance compliance to advance standardized cannabinoid therapies.

data.title: New Scientific Evidence Presented at ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 Strengthens the Case for Senzime's TetraGraph and Quantitative Neuromuscular Monitoring
data.description:
UPPSALA, SE AND SAN DIEGO, CA / ACCESS Newswire / October 17, 2026 / Senzime (STO:SEZI) (OTCQX:SNZZF) Senzime AB (publ), a global leader in precision-based patient monitoring solutions, today announced new scientific data presented at ANESTHESIOLOGY® 2026, the annual meeting of the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA). The research highlights important clinical and economic aspects of quantitative neuromuscular monitoring, including the benefits of Senzime's proprietary TetraGraph® technology.

The presentations follow a broad scientific and educational focus on neuromuscular management at this year's congress. More than 25 related sessions, scientific abstracts, quality improvement projects and clinical case presentations address topics ranging from quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and deep-block management to reversal strategies and postoperative outcomes.

"The breadth of neuromuscular management content at this year's ANESTHESIOLOGY meeting reflects how the science continues to evolve. The conversation is no longer about whether quantitative monitoring should be used, but how it can be used most effectively and integrated into everyday clinical practice," said Philip Siberg, CEO of Senzime. "We are proud to contribute new scientific evidence addressing two important dimensions of this evolution: helping clinicians gain more meaningful insights during deep neuromuscular block and helping hospitals better understand the clinical and economic benefits of implementing quantitative monitoring."

TetraGraph's automated deep-block monitoring technology demonstrates substantial improvements in monitoring performance
The study, "Effect of Adaptive Post-Tetanic Count Measurement on Effectiveness of Neuromuscular Monitoring during Deep Block," analyzed de-identified TetraGraph data from 9,938 surgical cases. The study evaluated TetraGraph's automated, patent-pending deep-block monitoring functionality, Adaptive PTC, and demonstrated substantial improvements in the depth and frequency of neuromuscular block assessment compared with conventional manual PTC activation. The abstract is authored by Sorin J. Brull, MD, FCARCSI (Hon), Julia Nordin, MSc, Jen Sanders, BSN, Linnea Troeng, MSc, Anders Jacobson, MSc, and Ammar Chadaideh, MSc.

New economic model demonstrates potential cost savings from quantitative neuromuscular monitoring
The study, "Cost Concerns of Quantitative Neuromuscular Monitoring-Developing a Return-on-Investment Calculator," introduces a customizable economic model designed to estimate the potential financial impact of implementing quantitative neuromuscular monitoring.

The model combines published rates of residual neuromuscular block and postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) with reversal drug costs and monitoring expenses to generate institution-specific economic estimates. In a modeled scenario involving 4,000 annual surgical cases requiring neuromuscular blocking agents and an increase in quantitative EMG monitoring adoption from 0% to 90%, the calculator estimated 32 fewer postoperative pulmonary complications annually, approximately $1.23 million in net annual savings after monitoring costs, and a break-even period of approximately 30 days.

These findings illustrate the potential economic value of broader quantitative neuromuscular monitoring adoption, while actual outcomes and savings will depend on individual hospital practices, patient populations and cost structures. The abstract is authored by Sorin J. Brull, MD, FCARCSI, and Michael J. Noble, MBA. It will be presented on Saturday, October 17, from 10:15 AM to 11:15 AM in the Exhibit Hall, ePosters Monitor 26.

Neuromuscular management takes center stage at ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026
The ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 scientific program features additional research and education addressing the adoption of quantitative monitoring, comparisons between electromyography (EMG) and acceleromyography (AMG), train-of-four documentation, optimization of reversal strategies, postoperative respiratory and pulmonary outcomes, and clinical cases illustrating the challenges of neuromuscular block management.

Several clinical experts who have collaborated with Senzime are also participating in the scientific program, contributing research and education on contemporary neuromuscular management. Their participation reflects the broader scientific dialogue on how quantitative monitoring can be implemented and optimized in clinical practice. These sessions are independently developed and are not sponsored or directed by Senzime.

For further information, please contact:
Philip Siberg, CEO of Senzime AB
Phone: +46 (0) 707 90 67 34, e-mail: philip.siberg@senzime.com

About Senzime
Senzime is a leading medical device company at the forefront of a changing healthcare market, driven by new clinical guidelines and emerging technologies. Established in 1999, Senzime develops and markets precision-based monitoring systems that improve outcomes, reduce costs, and advance perioperative patient safety. The flagship solution is the TetraGraph® system, proven best-in-class for accurate monitoring of neuromuscular transmission during surgery and used in thousands of operating rooms across the globe. The system helps to secure precise dosing of paralytic drugs and provides enhanced insights to safeguard every patient's journey, from anesthesia to recovery.

Headquartered in Uppsala, Sweden, Senzime is publicly traded on the Nasdaq Stockholm Main Market (SEZI), with cross-trading on the US OTCQX Market (SNZZF), and backed by long-term investors. More information is available at senzime.com.

data.title: 'Some people did everything right': I lost my home in the Great Recession. I rent in my 50s. Why is that judged as failure?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I earn $110,000 a year'

"Saving for a down payment is not easy in a major metropolitan area when a house costs three to four times your annual income." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I read the letter about mortgage applications and your response (As a mortgage loan officer, I rejected wealthy couples. Here's what can get your application declined.), and I agree with much of what this reader says. Living within your means, avoiding (unnecessary) debt and saving are good advice. There's a lot to be said for the discipline of "Joe Six-Pack," as the mortgage loan officer described him, who earns less but saves and eventually buys a home.

But there's another side of this that often gets overlooked - which, in fairness, you did address somewhat in your answer. I'm in my 50s, and the Great Recession hit at the worst time in my life. I wasn't a fool, but I did try to build a life for myself by buying a house. Still, the housing crash had consequences that lasted far longer than the recession itself. I lost my job and eventually my home. I earn $110,000 a year and it's still hard.

For people my age, getting knocked off the property ladder can be very hard to recover from. Those who already owned a home and held on to it through the downturn benefited enormously from the rise in property values that followed. Those who lost a home, sold at the wrong time or couldn't buy during those years missed out on that appreciation entirely. It was a matter of timing for many people, not reckless abandon as the mortgage loan officer would like us to believe.

Some people did everything right and were caught on the wrong side of an economic shock. Let me also tell you that saving for a down payment is not easy in a major metropolitan area when a house costs three to four times your annual income. So my message to your letter writer is to be careful about turning a lesson in spending too much into a judgment of people who haven't hit the same milestones. I am happy for friends and family who have homes, but it still stings.

Why judge other people for not getting on the property ladder?

Renter in His 50s

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: I'm 77, pay rent and live off Social Security, but I help homeless people. Why are so many people going hungry?

Homeownership in the U.S. has averaged 61% in Gallup polls since 2012, down from 70% between 2001 and 2011.

Dear Renter,

We are all on our own paths, and I'd bet that people who judge others for having less are insecure around those who have more.

You did not come out of the 2008-09 recession unscathed, and I can see why it rankles when somebody in a position of authority, even power, talks critically about would-be homebuyers putting too much money on credit cards or not saving enough of their salary, even though they earn a six-figure income. You have a right to feel the way you do, and you furthermore have a right to express it. I'm glad you chose to do that here.

For the record, the mortgage loan officer in question struck me as alarmist and at times judgmental. "People in the U.S. need to wake up and not be compulsive," she wrote. "Quit buying things you really don't need. It's that way with the federal government as well, and based on that, we'd better get real quick or we're going to have a financial crisis that makes the Great Recession of 2008 look like a picnic."

It's painful to have had a home once upon a time only to lose it, and to realize how much you lost. It was, sad to say, not an uncommon story during the last recession, when the unemployment rate rose to 10% and the number of foreclosure filings hit 2.8 million in 2009. I believe it helps enormously to know that this was a shared, collective trauma, and that many millions of people around the world also went through what you experienced.

Many millions of people around the world went through what you experienced.

High interest rates - the 30-year mortgage rate hit 7.3% in early October, nearly three times its level five years ago - and high house prices mean that buying a home remains out of reach for people who no longer have home equity to leverage, as well as for many first-time buyers. There's also a dearth of inventory in many markets, which has led to a generation of renters in their 30s, 40s, 50s and beyond. It can be a bitter pill to swallow.

At $110,000 a year, or $9,200 a month before taxes, lenders prefer housing costs at or below 30% of gross income. If you took a mortgage rate of 7.3%, even with money set aside for property taxes and insurance, you could afford a $300,000 property. That amount would be further reduced by student debt, a car payment and/or credit-card debt. And that's before you pull the money together for a down payment.

You would need to drum up $90,000 for a 20% down payment. That makes your task even more challenging after a job loss or foreclosure. Location matters too, as you say you live in a major metropolitan area. In the Midwest and South, $110,000 could buy a decent home, but in the New York, Boston, Los Angeles or Seattle areas, median prices can top $800,000, depending on the neighborhood.

Related: 'I don't want to die on the sales floor': I'm 67 and earn $19.50 an hour at a big-box store. When can I finally retire?

Homeownership rates have fallen

A recent Gallup poll shed light on what you are experiencing, and the results did not bode well for a generation of renters who would like to get their foot on the property ladder. The share of U.S. non-homeowners who expect to buy a home within five years has dropped to 25%, the lowest level Gallup has recorded since it began asking the question more than a decade ago. The poll found that 61% of Americans say they own their primary residence, while 34% rent.

Homeownership in the U.S. has averaged 61% in Gallup polls since 2012. Some 28% of non-homeowners told Gallup that they expect to buy a home within 10 years and just 25% said they expect to do so within five years, while 45% do not think they will do so at all in the foreseeable future. More worryingly, all of those figures have dropped over the past 10 years.

My colleagues Jillian Berman and Venessa Wong recently wrote about young Americans who feel shut out of the housing market - seemingly forever, in some cases. As they pointed out, the median age of renters in America now hovers around 42, up from 38 in 2006, and nearly one-third of renters have a college degree or higher, compared with 22% in 2010, according to Census Bureau data. Meanwhile, the national average rent is now $1,665 per month.

Renters are getting older, even if younger adults make up the largest share.

There has been some good news for renters. A 2026 report on rental housing from Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies said that after record-high increases during the pandemic, national rent growth has stayed near zero since mid-2023. Most markets experienced either small declines or small increases. In 74 of the largest 150 markets, asking rents fell, while 70 recorded modest growth of less than 4%. Rents rose by 4% or more in only six markets.

Perhaps the most significant takeaway is that renters are getting older, even if younger adults still make up the largest share of the renting population. Although there were roughly 6.1 million renters in your age group (50-59) in 2024, that number is down from 6.7 million in 2014. But there were more renters ages 60 to 69 (5.4 million versus 4.4 million in 2014) and 70 to 79 (3.4 million versus 2.3 million). That is a mixed picture at best.

Some 13% of renters are in their 50s, based on the most recent data from the U.S. Census Bureau. Adding up all those people from the JCHS report, 10.9 million people ages 60 and over are renters. That affects their financial security now and when they retire. Housing remains the biggest monthly expense for most people, and having to pay rent in your 60s does not make retirement any easier. Keep on saving and planning.

Take a bow. You are a survivor and, given the kind of upheaval you have endured, you are living a different kind of American dream.

Related: I'm 71 and still working. I earn $108,000 a year. Am I doing the right thing?

Check out The Moneyist's private Facebook group, where members help answer life's thorniest money issues. Post your questions, weigh in on the latest Moneyist columns or email The Moneyist on qfottrell@marketwatch.com.

data.title: Powering the AI Economy: New to The Street Show #776 Premieres Tonight on Bloomberg Television
data.description:
NEW YORK CITY, NY / ACCESS Newswire / October 17, 2026 / The race to power artificial intelligence is reshaping energy, storage, digital assets and even the way restaurants buy food. Tonight, New to The Street brings four companies working at the center of that shift to a global business audience as Show #776 premieres at 6:30 p.m. ET on Bloomberg Television as sponsored programming, with distribution across the United States, Latin America, the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) and Southeast Asia.

Hosted by Jane King, Show #776 features executive conversations with Brent Nelson, Executive Chairman of American Fusion Inc. (OTCQB:AMFN); Liam Phelan, who leads business development and sales at HPB (High Performance Battery); David McPhail, Chief Executive Officer of T-REX Acquisition Corp. (OTCQB:TRXA); and Alex Mouravieff, Co-Founder and CEO of SyncMeOn.

"Every company in this episode is answering a version of the same question: what does it take to run the next economy?" said Vince Caruso, Co-Founder and CEO of New to The Street. "Clean, compact power. Safer storage for data centers. Infrastructure for digital assets. Smarter supply chains for one of America's tightest-margin industries. These are stories investors in every region we reach want to hear, and that is exactly what our weekly Bloomberg footprint delivers. No politics. No current events. Only Opportunities To Consider™."

Inside Show #776

American Fusion Inc. (OTCQB:AMFN): "Basically, We Sell Power"
Executive Chairman Brent Nelson explains the Texatron™ Fusion Engine™, an aneutronic fusion platform designed for modular, infrastructure-grade deployment across industrial, commercial, defense and grid-constrained applications. Nelson describes a fuel cycle of deuterium and helium-3 that produces helium-4, with no radioactive waste, no meltdown risk, and no need to heat water or spin a turbine. He outlines the company's sales path from proposal to letter of intent to power purchase agreement, its focus on behind-the-meter data-center power, and remote, medical and military applications. Learn more at americanfusionenergy.com.

HPB (High Performance Battery): Bringing Solid-State Storage to U.S. Data Centers
Liam Phelan discusses HPB's international licensing model and its work toward a U.S. licensing partnership with BastionVolt Power focused on the data-center market. Phelan points to HPB's base of independent testing, including safety and abuse testing in Germany and extensive cycle-life data, and explains why safety, reliability and performance make data centers and backup power a natural fit for solid-state technology. He describes successful technology transfer as a true partnership: knowledge transfer, support through industrialization and production, and clear protection of HPB's intellectual property. Learn more at highperformancebattery.ch.

T-REX Acquisition Corp. (OTCQB:TRXA): Building Scale in Bitcoin Mining
CEO David McPhail shares his view that federal regulators, rather than new legislation, may provide the framework that brings traditional financial institutions into digital assets, and why he believes that validation could drive demand for Bitcoin's finite supply. McPhail updates viewers on the company's planned Georgia data-center acquisition, its engagement of an investment bank to raise up to $25 million to close the transaction and expand its mining footprint, and its goals heading into year-end and early 2027. Learn more at t-rexminingsolutions.com.

SyncMeOn: Modernizing How Restaurants Buy
Co-Founder and CEO Alex Mouravieff introduces SyncMeOn, an AI-powered marketplace and software platform connecting restaurants with food suppliers in real time. With restaurants keeping roughly three to four cents of every dollar they earn, Mouravieff explains how SyncMeOn gives operators price visibility and spending control, automates ordering from point-of-sale data, and flags anomalies before errors or fraud occur. The platform now lists more than 3,000 products in New York, has begun expanding into Connecticut, and plans further growth into Florida and other states. Learn more at syncmeon.com.

  • BioVie Inc. (NASDAQ:BIVI) - Phase 2 results for investigational oral therapy bezisterim in long COVID, which favored placebo on 21 of 22 endpoints overall; findings require confirmation in a Phase 3 trial
  • Lantern Pharma Inc. (NASDAQ:LTRN) - withZETA.ai, an AI platform designed to accelerate drug development for rare and hard-to-treat cancers
  • FreeCast (CAST) - a unified streaming gateway aggregating free and premium content into one platform

Why: Rosen Law Firm, a global investor rights law firm, reminds purchasers of common stock of Doximity, Inc. (NYSE: DOCS) between August 8, 2024 and May 13, 2026, both dates inclusive (the "Class Period"), of the important November 16, 2026 lead plaintiff deadline.

data.title: Meet the home buyers totally unfazed by 7% mortgage rates
data.description:
By Aarthi Swaminathan

Individual investors and second-home buyers accounted for 1 in 5 home purchases in September - the highest share in a little over a year

While mortgage rates over 7% have everyday house hunters pulling back from the market, data suggest that real-estate investors are sticking it out.

In June, real-estate investor Justin Smith closed on a duplex in Roscoe, Ill. - about 90 miles west of Chicago - for $250,000. The rate on his 30-year fixed mortgage was 7%.

Smith, a 34-year-old real-estate broker who also owns three apartment buildings in Roscoe and nearby Rockford, told MarketWatch that smaller Midwestern cities in particular offer an easy way into real-estate investing, because the barrier to entry - namely, home prices - is relatively low. The average home value in Rockford, Ill., is about $185,000, according to Zillow's (Z) (ZG) estimates, compared to a national median value of about $366,000.

More importantly, "we have such a strong rental population," Smith said, meaning that many people in the area rent instead of own.

Smith isn't the only real-estate investor who's buying right now. While surging mortgage rates over 7% have everyday house hunters pulling back from the market, data suggest that real-estate investors are sticking it out.

In September, individual investors and second-home buyers accounted for 20% of home-purchase transactions - the highest share in a little over a year, according to the National Association of Realtors.

"Investors tend to pull back less than noninvestor buyers when conditions deteriorate," Hannah Jones, a senior economist at Realtor.com, told MarketWatch. "So their share of total buyers rises as higher mortgage rates squeeze out more noninvestor buyers." (Realtor.com is operated by News Corp subsidiary Move Inc.; MarketWatch publisher Dow Jones is also a subsidiary of News Corp.)

"There are opportunities for investors today that we haven't seen in years. Inventory is rising, sellers are cutting prices and negotiating leverage is shifting toward buyers," Michael Carbonare, another real-estate investor, told MarketWatch.

In September, the total for-sale housing inventory in the U.S. jumped to 1.6 million units, the highest level since November 2019, NAR said. About 43% of sellers were cutting prices as of Oct. 12, according to separate data from ParclHQ.

"It's a good time to be looking for motivated sellers, buying right and structuring deals that make financial sense," Carbonare said.

Related: U.S. wealth has shifted to stocks from homes. There are big reasons to worry.

Relatively small-time real-estate investors - those who own three to nine properties - have been more active than large landlords. About 14.5% of home purchases made in August were by smaller real-estate investors, which was up from 13.6% a year ago, according to Cotality, a real-estate data-analytics company.

In contrast, 9% of purchases were by medium-sized investors, and 2% were by large investors.

One factor driving some investors to buy houses now is strong rental demand. Rents nationally are trending upwards: In September, the typical rent rose 2.7% from the same time a year ago to around $1,900, Zillow found in an analysis.

"Elevated mortgage rates have pushed home shoppers straight into the arms of rentals," Kara Ng, a senior economist at Zillow, said in the report.

The company estimated that demand for single-family rentals rose nearly 22% in September from the previous year, and 10% for multifamily or apartment rentals.

In Chicago, where the typical rent grew 4.7% in September from last year to about $2,200, according to Zillow, 66-year-old Tom Moran is putting down $500,000 for a $2 million, six-unit apartment building in the city - the latest addition to his portfolio of 18 other buildings.

The mortgage rate was 6.625% for the bank-portfolio loan Moran used to finance the purchase, though he said the rate wasn't a concern for him. "It's just a number," Moran, a real-estate investor and broker who is now under contract on the property, told MarketWatch.

"Interest rates go up, interest rates go down - but in general, real estate is a long-term buy," he said. "I look at real estate as basically like a little business ... so I'm not worried about the initial return."

Having bought his first property in the late 1980s when the 30-year mortgage rate averaged over 10%, Moran said he's accustomed to high-rate environments.

As part of his due diligence before his latest purchase, Moran called up a few mortgage lenders for quotes before he pulled the trigger. The rates he was quoted ranged from mid-6% to over 7% - but he said he was unfazed.

"People freak out" when they see the 7% handle, Moran noted. On the loan he was pursuing, the rate going up a quarter point, from 6.875% to 7.125%, amounted to a roughly $250 hit per month for him. "It's not a deal-breaker," he said.

Do you have questions about real estate and home-buying that you would like to see covered in MarketWatch? We'd love to hear from you. You can write to us at readerstories@marketwatch.com. A reporter may be in touch to learn more. MarketWatch will not attribute your answers to you by name without your permission.

-Aarthi Swaminathan

data.title: 'Some people did everything right': I lost my home in the Great Recession. I rent in my 50s. Why is that judged as failure?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I earn $110,000 a year'

"Saving for a down payment is not easy in a major metropolitan area when a house costs three to four times your annual income." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I read the letter about mortgage applications and your response (As a mortgage loan officer, I rejected wealthy couples. Here's what can get your application declined.), and I agree with much of what this reader says. Living within your means, avoiding (unnecessary) debt and saving are good advice. There's a lot to be said for the discipline of "Joe Six-Pack," as the mortgage loan officer described him, who earns less but saves and eventually buys a home.

But there's another side of this that often gets overlooked - which, in fairness, you did address somewhat in your answer. I'm in my 50s, and the Great Recession hit at the worst time in my life. I wasn't a fool, but I did try to build a life for myself by buying a house. Still, the housing crash had consequences that lasted far longer than the recession itself. I lost my job and eventually my home. I earn $110,000 a year and it's still hard.

For people my age, getting knocked off the property ladder can be very hard to recover from. Those who already owned a home and held on to it through the downturn benefited enormously from the rise in property values that followed. Those who lost a home, sold at the wrong time or couldn't buy during those years missed out on that appreciation entirely. It was a matter of timing for many people, not reckless abandon as the mortgage loan officer would like us to believe.

Some people did everything right and were caught on the wrong side of an economic shock. Let me also tell you that saving for a down payment is not easy in a major metropolitan area when a house costs three to four times your annual income. So my message to your letter writer is to be careful about turning a lesson in spending too much into a judgment of people who haven't hit the same milestones. I am happy for friends and family who have homes, but it still stings.

Why judge other people for not getting on the property ladder?

Renter in His 50s

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: I'm 77, pay rent and live off Social Security, but I help homeless people. Why are so many people going hungry?

Homeownership in the U.S. has averaged 61% in Gallup polls since 2012, down from 70% between 2001 and 2011.

Dear Renter,

We are all on our own paths, and I'd bet that people who judge others for having less are insecure around those who have more.

You did not come out of the 2008-09 recession unscathed, and I can see why it rankles when somebody in a position of authority, even power, talks critically about would-be homebuyers putting too much money on credit cards or not saving enough of their salary, even though they earn a six-figure income. You have a right to feel the way you do, and you furthermore have a right to express it. I'm glad you chose to do that here.

For the record, the mortgage loan officer in question struck me as alarmist and at times judgmental. "People in the U.S. need to wake up and not be compulsive," she wrote. "Quit buying things you really don't need. It's that way with the federal government as well, and based on that, we'd better get real quick or we're going to have a financial crisis that makes the Great Recession of 2008 look like a picnic."

It's painful to have had a home once upon a time only to lose it, and to realize how much you lost. It was, sad to say, not an uncommon story during the last recession, when the unemployment rate rose to 10% and the number of foreclosure filings hit 2.8 million in 2009. I believe it helps enormously to know that this was a shared, collective trauma, and that many millions of people around the world also went through what you experienced.

Many millions of people around the world went through what you experienced.

High interest rates - the 30-year mortgage rate hit 7.3% in early October, nearly three times its level five years ago - and high house prices mean that buying a home remains out of reach for people who no longer have home equity to leverage, as well as for many first-time buyers. There's also a dearth of inventory in many markets, which has led to a generation of renters in their 30s, 40s, 50s and beyond. It can be a bitter pill to swallow.

At $110,000 a year, or $9,200 a month before taxes, lenders prefer housing costs at or below 30% of gross income. If you took a mortgage rate of 7.3%, even with money set aside for property taxes and insurance, you could afford a $300,000 property. That amount would be further reduced by student debt, a car payment and/or credit-card debt. And that's before you pull the money together for a down payment.

You would need to drum up $90,000 for a 20% down payment. That makes your task even more challenging after a job loss or foreclosure. Location matters too, as you say you live in a major metropolitan area. In the Midwest and South, $110,000 could buy a decent home, but in the New York, Boston, Los Angeles or Seattle areas, median prices can top $800,000, depending on the neighborhood.

Related: 'I don't want to die on the sales floor': I'm 67 and earn $19.50 an hour at a big-box store. When can I finally retire?

Homeownership rates have fallen

A recent Gallup poll shed light on what you are experiencing, and the results did not bode well for a generation of renters who would like to get their foot on the property ladder. The share of U.S. non-homeowners who expect to buy a home within five years has dropped to 25%, the lowest level Gallup has recorded since it began asking the question more than a decade ago. The poll found that 61% of Americans say they own their primary residence, while 34% rent.

Homeownership in the U.S. has averaged 61% in Gallup polls since 2012. Some 28% of non-homeowners told Gallup that they expect to buy a home within 10 years and just 25% said they expect to do so within five years, while 45% do not think they will do so at all in the foreseeable future. More worryingly, all of those figures have dropped over the past 10 years.

My colleagues Jillian Berman and Venessa Wong recently wrote about young Americans who feel shut out of the housing market - seemingly forever, in some cases. As they pointed out, the median age of renters in America now hovers around 42, up from 38 in 2006, and nearly one-third of renters have a college degree or higher, compared with 22% in 2010, according to Census Bureau data. Meanwhile, the national average rent is now $1,665 per month.

Renters are getting older, even if younger adults make up the largest share.

There has been some good news for renters. A 2026 report on rental housing from Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies said that after record-high increases during the pandemic, national rent growth has stayed near zero since mid-2023. Most markets experienced either small declines or small increases. In 74 of the largest 150 markets, asking rents fell, while 70 recorded modest growth of less than 4%. Rents rose by 4% or more in only six markets.

Perhaps the most significant takeaway is that renters are getting older, even if younger adults still make up the largest share of the renting population. Although there were roughly 6.1 million renters in your age group (50-59) in 2024, that number is down from 6.7 million in 2014. But there were more renters ages 60 to 69 (5.4 million versus 4.4 million in 2014) and 70 to 79 (3.4 million versus 2.3 million). That is a mixed picture at best.

Some 13% of renters are in their 50s, based on the most recent data from the U.S. Census Bureau. Adding up all those people from the JCHS report, 10.9 million people ages 60 and over are renters. That affects their financial security now and when they retire. Housing remains the biggest monthly expense for most people, and having to pay rent in your 60s does not make retirement any easier. Keep on saving and planning.

Take a bow. You are a survivor and, given the kind of upheaval you have endured, you are living a different kind of American dream.

Related: I'm 71 and still working. I earn $108,000 a year. Am I doing the right thing?

NEW YORK, Oct. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Faruqi & Faruqi, LLP, a leading national securities law firm, is investigating potential claims against Innventure, Inc. ("Innventure" or the "Company") (NASDAQ: INV) and reminds investors of the October 27, 2026 deadline to seek the role of lead plaintiff in a federal securities class action that has been filed against the Company.

Faruqi & Faruqi is a leading national securities law firm with offices in New York, Pennsylvania, California and Georgia. The firm has recovered hundreds of millions of dollars for investors since its founding in 1995. See www.faruqilaw.com.

As detailed below, the complaint alleges that the Company and its executives violated federal securities laws by making false and/or misleading statements and/or failing to disclose that: (1) Accelsius' alleged transformative deal with DarkNX was unlikely to come to fruition as no evidence of DarkNX constructing or facilitating a large scale AI data center existed; (2) as a result, the Company's stated revenue and cash flow targets for Accelsius in 2026 were overstated; and (3) that, as a result of the foregoing, Defendants' positive statements about the Company's business, operations, and prospects were materially misleading and/or lacked a reasonable basis.

On May 28, 2026, before the market opened, Morpheus Research published a report alleging that Innventure's DarkNX venture to build an AI data center campus in Ontario was a fabrication. The report revealed there was "zero evidence this project exists or that DarkNX has the team or funding to even contemplate such a project." Morpheus Research further reported that "[a]ccording to a former Innventure executive, management was using 'false information' and revenue projections that were 'pure fiction' to solicit investments into Accelsius." The report quoted multiple former Accelsius employees, who stated, among other things, "we've never heard of the company [DarkNX], they don't have customers, there's no data center."

On this news, Innventure's stock price fell $0.54 per share, or 8.42%, to close at $5.87 per share on May 28, 2026, on unusually heavy trading volume.

On August 13, 2026, after the market closed, Innventure reported second quarter 2026 results. Among other items, Innventure disclosed a net loss of $34.9 million, compared to $27.8 million in the first quarter of 2026, and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $22.6 million, compared to $18.4 million in the first quarter of 2026. The Company also announced it is "suspending [its] previously communicated expectations regarding Accelsius' 2026 revenue and cash flow targets and shifting [its] focus."

On the same day, Innventure filed its quarterly report on Form 10-Q with the SEC, disclosing that "the deployment site identified in the DarkNX purchase order is no longer available. Accelsius has removed the DarkNX project from its internal bookings."

On this news, Innventure's stock price fell $1.98 per share, or 55%, to close at $1.62 per share on August 14, 2026, on unusually heavy trading volume.
